::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: A considerable proportion of the global adult population is bilingual; however, research on aphasia and language processing remains predominantly centered on monolingual speakers, leading to reduced understanding and guidance about bilingual aphasia.
Bilingual aphasia is not equivalent to monolingual aphasia, as bilinguals process each language differently from monolinguals.
As such, they are likely to have different error patterns and recovery processes.
Best practice for assessing bilingual individuals with aphasia requires evaluating all languages they have sufficiently acquired.

Because standardized normative tools are not available for many language combinations or even for numerous individual languages, clinicians can derive necessary insights into a bilingual patient's linguistic strengths and impairments through systematic discourse sampling.
Consequently, we provide best practice recommendations for assessing and treating discourse production in bilingual aphasia.

We synthesize current practices in language assessment and treatment of discourse production for bilingual aphasia populations, and provide clinically applicable recommendations for selecting, administering, coding, and interpreting discourse assessments across languages.
We also provide recommendations for selecting and adapting discourse interventions, treatment languages, and cross-language targets within the constraints of multilingual clinical service delivery.
An ever-increasing proportion of the world population is acquiring and using more than one language variety (Bialystok et al., 2009; Grosjean, 1989).

text.text: In the context of bilingual aphasia, this paper defines a bilingual individual as anyone who has achieved at least an intermediate proficiency in two or more language varieties at any point in their life.

This clinical definition concerns language acquisition and its potential neurocognitive consequences, rather than whether an individual identifies as bilingual (Arce Rentería et al., 2026; Wagner et al., 2022).

text.text: As a result, even healthy bilinguals process all of their languages differently from monolinguals, so it is not uncommon for bilinguals to make non-native-like judgments in their first or dominant language(s) (e.g., Jegerski et al., 2016).

text.text: In addition, healthy bilinguals often mix their languages when speaking to listeners who comprehend their languages, a phenomenon called codeswitching or code mixing (Heredia & Altarriba, 2001; Meisel, 1994; Myers-Scotton, 2020; Toribio, 2001).

text.text: This healthy phenomenon can occur across various linguistic levels including discourse, morpheme boundaries, and phoneme targets, among others.
Bilinguals may also supplant words or structures from a stronger to a weaker language in situations where they are unsure what to say.

While these non-native-like language processing patterns in their languages are sometimes misinterpreted as deficits, improvements to metalinguistic awareness or executive control (Altman et al., 2018; Bialystok et al., 2014; Cummins, 1978; Galambos & Hakuta, 1988; Lehtonen et al., 2018) show that bilingualism is a net positive for individuals' brains.

text.text: Advocates for bilingual aphasia populations champion integrating this understanding into a translanguaging framework, which highlights evaluating communication abilities across an individual's entire linguistic repertoire rather than treating language as distinct systems (Bortz & Goral, 2025).

text.text: In a recent study, Goral et al. (2025) reported that assessing language performance across all languages yields more accurate and ecologically valid reflections of an individual's communication ability.

text.text: Overall, this approach recognizes that multilingual speakers strategically blend languages, and assessing this behavior can reveal preserved language strengths that might otherwise be missed.
Furthermore, the translanguaging framework promotes capturing realworld, functional communication and guides treatment that is meaningful for everyday functioning.
Therefore, bilingual patients, in any context, should be assessed in each language they know.
However, normative assessments are not available for bilinguals in each language pair or even monolinguals in each language (Wallace et al., 2022).

text.text: As such, we recommend determining strengths and limitations of bilingual people with aphasia (bPWA) in each language through discourse sampling.
Discourse is defined as ''a language unit whose organization supersedes any single word or sentence'' (Olness, 2006, p. 176).
text.formatted: Discourse is defined as ''a language unit whose organization supersedes any single word or sentence'' <ref type="bibr">(Olness, 2006, p. 176)</ref>.

text.text: Discourse production involves integrating lexical, syntactic, semantic, and pragmatic processes across contexts (Alyahya et al., 2020).

text.text: Discourse samples may provide a more holistic and naturalistic assessment, making them preferable even when impairment-based normative assessments are available for bilingual populations (Alyahya, Lambon Ralph, et al., 2022; Bose et al., 2026; Dutta et al., 2025; Stark, 2019; Stark et al., 2023).

text.text: Likewise, treatment of discourse may provide patients with enhanced skills for functional communication (Ansaldo & Saidi, 2014; Dipper et al., 2021; Faroqi-Shah et al., 2010).

text.text: Guidelines for assessing and/or treating discourse production for bPWA do not currently exist.

Accordingly, the aim of this paper is to provide these guidelines: best practices for the identification of a bilingual individual with aphasia, and their subsequent assessment and treatment of discourse production.
At the onset of any assessment, clinicians (i.e., speech-language pathologists/therapists) must gather background information about their patient.
At this time, clinicians should determine whether their patient is bilingual, as bilingual patients will have different language performance than monolingual patients.

To determine if a patient is bilingual, the clinician should ask every patient (and, when appropriate, their family) whether the patient has acquired and used another language to at least an intermediate level at any point in life, including languages that are no longer used regularly, and about the contexts in which those languages were acquired and used (cf. Birdsong et al., 2012).

text.text: Asking only whether someone is "bilingual," "is fluent" in another language, or uses more than one language daily is insufficient because selfidentification may not reflect their holistic language experience (Wagner et al., 2022).

text.text: Bilingualism isn't a monolithic category though; if the patient is bilingual, clinicians should delve deeper to determine their patient's type of bilingualism.

And while it is widely reported that knowing a patient's first or dominant language will predict recovery patterns (i.e., Ribot's or Pitres' laws), the evidence to support those claims is insufficient (Pearce, 2005), while the wider body of evidence suggests that the recovery patterns of bilinguals vary (Peñaloza & Kiran, 2019).

text.text: If a clinician determines that a patient is bilingual, they need to gather additional information about the patient's type of bilingualism, the languages they speak, the age at which they first began acquiring the second language(s), their pre-morbid proficiency, and their language dominance (Grosjean, 1989; Surrain & Luk, 2019).

text.text: These factors are particularly important to note because they are known to affect the cortical and mental organization of bilinguals' languages and may manifest in markedly different language behaviors for different groups of bilinguals.
These behavioral differences, which are not clinical findings, should be predicted by clinicians so that they are not confused with aphasia deficits.
Many predictions about bilinguals' processing can be made merely from comparing the languages' structures.
There are over 7000 documented languages (Eberhard et al., 2025), with hundreds of different structures in a given language (Haspelmath et al., 2005).
text.formatted: There are over 7000 documented languages <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Eberhard et al., 2025)</ref>, with hundreds of different structures in a given language <ref type="bibr">(Haspelmath et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Languages are traditionally compared phylogenetically (i.e., how the languages relate to one another historically), but such a comparison would not be useful for clinicians in decision making, as the historical relationship between two languages does not predict whether a given language structure is the same or similar between languages.
For example, knowing that English and German are historically related Germanic languages is not useful for a clinician in understanding bilinguals' processing or perception of the languages.
On the other hand, if a language structure is partially overlapping between languages, a bilingual may process it at a level between that of monolingual speakers of those languages.
For example, Italian-English bilinguals have been shown to produce vowels that are halfway between the acoustic qualities of English and Italian vowels (Flege et al., 2003).
text.formatted: For example, Italian-English bilinguals have been shown to produce vowels that are halfway between the acoustic qualities of English and Italian vowels <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Flege et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Beneficial overlap can occur when languages have no historical relationship.

For example, Japanese and English share word forms (e.g., スーツケース "Sūtsukēsu" / 'suitcase'), called cognates, which are processed faster and more accurately than words without overlap by Japanese-English bilinguals (Hoshino & Kroll, 2008).

text.text: The relationship between bilinguals' languages is further affected by their individual combination of background factors, particularly the age at which they first began to acquire their L2 known as the age of acquisition (AoA), their proficiency levels, and their usage patterns (Bialystok et al., 2009; Surrain & Luk, 2019).

text.text: Individuals who begin acquiring 2+ languages from birth, simultaneous bilinguals, may show differences in neural organization relative to bilinguals with later ages of acquisition (Perani et al., 1998; Pliatsikas et al., 2015).

text.text: Since they have received language input in more than one language at an early age, the organization of their languages, mentally and cortically, may be more distinct (Kousaie et al., 2017; Roesch & Chondrogianni, 2016).
text.formatted: Since they have received language input in more than one language at an early age, the organization of their languages, mentally and cortically, may be more distinct <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">(Kousaie et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b135">Roesch & Chondrogianni, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Some simultaneous bilinguals produce non-native-like sentences in one or more of their languages, and may have a non-native accent in either language (Hopp & Schmid, 2013; Kupisch et al., 2014).

text.text: Similarly, children who begin acquiring an L2 very early, sequential bilinguals, may have stronger neural connections between languages (Perani et al., 1998; Pliatsikas et al., 2015), but similarly may demonstrate non-native-like performance in either language.

text.text: In particular, early sequential bilinguals or simultaneous bilinguals who speak a minority language at home, heritage speakers, may have limited exposure to that language elsewhere and are at risk of not acquiring lower frequency structures due to limited input or chances for conversational practice (which reinforces input) (Montrul, 2010; Polinsky & Scontras, 2020).
text.formatted: In particular, early sequential bilinguals or simultaneous bilinguals who speak a minority language at home, heritage speakers, may have limited exposure to that language elsewhere and are at risk of not acquiring lower frequency structures due to limited input or chances for conversational practice (which reinforces input) <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">(Montrul, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b131">Polinsky & Scontras, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, many heritage speakers have relatively strong comprehension skills but significantly weaker production skills.

This may also be the result of heritage speakers attending mainstream schools and feeling social pressure to speak only the majority language, leading them to refuse to use the minority language, further affecting their proficiency (Cummins, 1978).
text.formatted: This may also be the result of heritage speakers attending mainstream schools and feeling social pressure to speak only the majority language, leading them to refuse to use the minority language, further affecting their proficiency <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Cummins, 1978)</ref>.

text.text: Relatedly, heritage speakers are often intersectionally ethno-racial minorities who face wider social bias and discrimination (Cummins, 1978; Genesee, 2006).
text.formatted: Relatedly, heritage speakers are often intersectionally ethno-racial minorities who face wider social bias and discrimination <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Cummins, 1978;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Genesee, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, child heritage speakers typically encounter educational barriers and obstacles leading to lower educational attainment, despite the likely higher metacognitive and metalinguistic abilities than their peers, afforded by their bilingualism.
Language testing of heritage speakers may show weaker proficiency, particularly in their first language (L1), but still show crosslinguistic influence (Montrul, 2010).
text.formatted: Language testing of heritage speakers may show weaker proficiency, particularly in their first language (L1), but still show crosslinguistic influence <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">(Montrul, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, their neurophysiological testing should position them with other bilinguals of similar acquisition timeframes (Bialystok et al., 2009; Duñabeitia et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Nevertheless, their neurophysiological testing should position them with other bilinguals of similar acquisition timeframes <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Bialystok et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Duñabeitia et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, clinicians should consider age with context of acquisition in determining potential effects on their patient, in order to determine whether language differences are due to interlanguage influence or incomplete acquisition (which are normal bilingualism effects), or deficits resulting from aphasia.
Clearly, AoA can affect proficiency levels, since many individuals who begin acquiring a new language will not attain native-like behavioral performance.
The acquisition or learning process can plateau at any stage and for a variety of reasons, even in healthy populations.

For example, a child may emigrate with family to a country where one language is no longer spoken, or an adult may discontinue language classes that were progressing their skills in complex grammar structures.
If a person acquires aphasia prior to attaining native-like communication skills, they clearly should not be judged the same way as native speakers.
However, awareness of the acquisition process is important even when a patient is an advanced speaker in an L2.
The sequence of acquisition for language structures is not always intuitive and depends on when a learner began acquiring language, as well as how similar their languages are.

When someone began acquiring an L2 as a child, particularly in earlier adolescence, they may have incompletely acquired the L1, resulting in swifter L2 acquisition (Hopp & Schmid, 2013; Kupisch et al., 2014; Polinsky & Scontras, 2020).
text.formatted: When someone began acquiring an L2 as a child, particularly in earlier adolescence, they may have incompletely acquired the L1, resulting in swifter L2 acquisition <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Hopp & Schmid, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Kupisch et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b131">Polinsky & Scontras, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: On the other hand, when someone begins acquiring a new language as an adult, they will have less difficulty with language structures that are similar between their L1 and new L2 (or possibly the same between the new L2 and other previously learned languages) (Cho & Slabakova, 2014).
text.formatted: On the other hand, when someone begins acquiring a new language as an adult, they will have less difficulty with language structures that are similar between their L1 and new L2 (or possibly the same between the new L2 and other previously learned languages) <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Cho & Slabakova, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Structures that are completely novel as well as structures with a partial overlap across languages will be more difficult to acquire, such as the plural system in Spanish for native English speakers (Zagona, 2002).
text.formatted: Structures that are completely novel as well as structures with a partial overlap across languages will be more difficult to acquire, such as the plural system in Spanish for native English speakers <ref type="bibr" target="#b157">(Zagona, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Many of the language structures that are acquired later also mirror those considered in language assessments of aphasia deficits, such as the copula 'be' in English.
Similarly, some cues, like word order, which are crucial in English, may hold little value in another language.
Also, cues that are not possible in English may be important to use in other languages.
In some languages, the frequency of canonical structures (e.g., active voice) also varies across languages.
So, clinicians must make careful consideration of which structures had (not) been (fully) acquired for determining which structures are affected by a patient's aphasia.
Relatedly, individuals with incomplete acquisition as well as those comfortable in the language, may switch between the L2 and any other language.
Those with incomplete acquisition may fill gaps in word knowledge or appropriate grammatical structures by using those from another language.
Still, bilinguals may use multiple languages in a discourse context when their communication partner speaks more than one of their languages as well (Ansaldo & Marcotte, 2007; Mooijman et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Still, bilinguals may use multiple languages in a discourse context when their communication partner speaks more than one of their languages as well <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Ansaldo & Marcotte, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b117">Mooijman et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Switching between languages when a patient has aphasia should be considered parasitic switching when the patient has no ability to control which language they use.
This would happen when a patient's language control is affected.
Language control is part of the executive control network, separate from the language network in the brain.
Bilingual aphasia patients who switch may not be aware they are switching languages, indicating impaired language control (Gray & Kiran, 2016; Green & Abutalebi, 2008; Kuzmina et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Bilingual aphasia patients who switch may not be aware they are switching languages, indicating impaired language control <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Gray & Kiran, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Green & Abutalebi, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Kuzmina et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Clinicians should consider impacts on language control by assessing patients in monolingual and bilingual contexts, and/or by asking patients if they are aware of their switches in switching contexts.
To collect bilingual background factors for patients, clinicians can conduct interviews or ask family members.

Validated language history questionnaires such as the Bilingual Language Profile (BLP; Birdsong et al., 2012), the Language Experience and Proficiency Questionnaire (LEAP-Q; Marian et al., 2007), and the Language and Social Background Questionnaire (LSBQ; Anderson et al., 2018) can assist clinicians in identifying bilingual language backgrounds.

text.text: When validated questionnaires are available, they should be prioritized over tools without established measurement properties and supplemented as needed with informal interviews with the patient and family members.
These instruments collect data on multidimensional constructs such as AoA, language use, exposure patterns, and educational history, all of which shape the dynamic nature of bilingualism.

text.text: Overall, a few key-points that clinicians need to consider when collecting the pre-stroke language history are: 1) they should select the questionnaire which aligns best with their clinical questions and assessment goals; and 2) clinicians should use multiple tools to collect a comprehensive premorbid language profile of their bilingual patients.

Conventional diagnostic tests are often developed for monolingual speakers; if they are not normed for bilingual populations, they may over-or under-estimate language deficits and fail to account for interlanguage influence.

Language assessments such as the Western Aphasia Battery (WAB; Kertesz, 2007), the Boston Naming Test (BNT; Kaplan et al., 2001), and the Comprehensive Aphasia Test (CAT; Swinburn et al., 2004), have translated or adapted versions.

text.text: Equivalence across languages requires cultural, linguistic, and psychometric adaptation rather than direct translation alone (Alyahya, 2024), however, the absence of full equivalence does not make these tools clinically useless.

text.text: When no fully adapted and normed instrument is available, a translated or partially adapted measure may still provide useful structured information, provided that clinicians do not apply inappropriate norms and interpret the findings alongside discourse samples, language-history information, and other converging evidence.
Continued development and norming of language-specific adaptations are needed, although comprehensive coverage of all languages and language varieties may never be feasible.
Even when a traditional assessment is adapted to a larger number of language pairs, not all pairs will have been considered in the innumerable possible bilingual pairs.
For example, the Bilingual Aphasia Test (BAT; Paradis, 1987) was designed to assess two languages of a bilingual person with aphasia (bPWA) equivalently and is available in 65 languages.

text.text: Similarly, the Comprehensive Aphasia Test (CAT; Swinburn et al., 2004) has been adapted in various European languages.

text.text: Although standardized aphasia batteries may include connected-speech components, they generally provide limited sampling across discourse tasks, languages, and interactional contexts.

Additional discourse sampling can therefore provide converging evidence across tasks and languages that helps clinicians distinguish language impairment from task-, language-, and culture-related variation.
When a clinician selects discourse as the mode of assessment for bPWA, there are a few factors to consider.
First, bPWA must be evaluated in all the languages proficiently acquired.
Furthermore, the discourse tasks should elicit structures relevant to interlanguage influence and cross-linguistic generalization, as well as be culturally appropriate.
Task selection should also align with the specific linguistic domains most relevant to the individual's aphasia profile, including aphasia type and severity, if known.
Advantages: Allows collection of retrospective selfreports on AoA, language use, educational history, and self-rated language abilities.

Disadvantages: Retrospective self-reports may introduce recall bias or inaccuracies; scoring procedures, questionnaire content, and availability of normative or reference data vary across instruments.

Bilingual Aphasia Test (BAT) Advantages: Sensitive tool for bilingual aphasia, culturally and linguistically appropriate across multiple language pairs, evaluates broad range of language domains and modalities.
Disadvantages: Constrained clinical utility (limited number of items per subtest, absence of composite domain scores or overall aphasia severity score).
Comprehensive Aphasia Test (CAT) Advantages: Multidimensional -assesses language, cognition, quality of life, provides overall aphasia severity score.
Disadvantages: Effectiveness depends on availability of fully validated versions.

text.text: This source even allows direct comparison of 2 languages.

In considering the similarities of 2 languages, clinicians should reflect on whether a given structure overlaps across more than one language, is completely different (e.g., including existing in only one language), or is partially overlapping (Cho & Slabakova, 2014).
text.formatted: In considering the similarities of 2 languages, clinicians should reflect on whether a given structure overlaps across more than one language, is completely different (e.g., including existing in only one language), or is partially overlapping <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Cho & Slabakova, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: For example, in a comparison of Spanish and English, both languages are exactly the same in the base sentence structure (subject-verb-object), completely different in noun grammatical gender (English does not mark nouns by gender), and partially overlapping in noun plural structure (Spanish marks the article and adjectives with the plural marker while English only marks the noun) (Zagona, 2002).
text.formatted: For example, in a comparison of Spanish and English, both languages are exactly the same in the base sentence structure (subject-verb-object), completely different in noun grammatical gender (English does not mark nouns by gender), and partially overlapping in noun plural structure (Spanish marks the article and adjectives with the plural marker while English only marks the noun) <ref type="bibr" target="#b157">(Zagona, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: The clinician would not need to examine these overlap levels for all the possible grammar structures and features.
Instead they should pay particular attention to structures that have partial overlap but are used frequently.

This is because fully overlapping structures will be strongest in the minds of any bilinguals, while partially overlapping structures will have relatively weaker representations (Cho & Slabakova, 2014).
text.formatted: This is because fully overlapping structures will be strongest in the minds of any bilinguals, while partially overlapping structures will have relatively weaker representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Cho & Slabakova, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The strength or weakness of those representations premorbidly depends upon the individual's age and context of acquisition, proficiency, and patterns of language use.
WALS provides an accessible starting point for identifying cross-linguistic structural similarities and differences, although coverage varies across languages and linguistic features.
When information for a particular language or structure is unavailable, clinicians can supplement WALS with reference grammars or consultation with a language specialist (Dryer & Haspelmath, 2013).
text.formatted: When information for a particular language or structure is unavailable, clinicians can supplement WALS with reference grammars or consultation with a language specialist <ref type="bibr">(Dryer & Haspelmath, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: These structural comparisons can guide the selection of discourse tasks that elicit clinically relevant linguistic features.
Different discourse genres used with aphasia populations are commonly classified as descriptive, narrative, procedural, personal, expository, and conversational.
Language performance can vary across genres and tasks (Alyahya et al., 2020; Alyahya, Lambon Ralph, et al., 2022; Bryant et al., 2016; Stark, 2019).
text.formatted: Language performance can vary across genres and tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Alyahya et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Alyahya, Lambon Ralph, et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Bryant et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b142">Stark, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: While genres are the forms or types of discourse with specific communicative purpose (e.g., a narration, conversation), tasks are the specific activities (e.g., storytelling, picture description) or prompts (e.g., 'tell me about your day so far', 'describe this picture') used to elicit discourse.
One genre of discourse can be elicited using different tasks.
As discourse performance varies with genre and tasks (Stark, 2019; Stark & Fukuyama, 2021), clinicians should consider the structures of interest in selecting the genre/task.
text.formatted: As discourse performance varies with genre and tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b142">(Stark, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b145">Stark & Fukuyama, 2021)</ref>, clinicians should consider the structures of interest in selecting the genre/task.

text.text: Conversation is an important discourse paradigm because it samples language during interactive communication rather than monologic production.
It can be elicited through structured prompts or sampled from unstructured interaction, and the conversation partner need not be the clinician.

Depending on the clinical question, partners may include the clinician, a family member or other familiar communication partner, or another interlocutor; these contexts may provide different information about functional communication.

Because conversational performance is co-constructed, clinicians should document who participated and the partner's relationship to the patient and, when direct cross-language comparison is intended, consider whether differences in partner or interactional context could contribute to performance (Leaman & Edmonds, 2019 , 2021).
text.formatted: Because conversational performance is co-constructed, clinicians should document who participated and the partner's relationship to the patient and, when direct cross-language comparison is intended, consider whether differences in partner or interactional context could contribute to performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">(Leaman & Edmonds, 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, clinicians should employ multiple task types to elicit naturalistic communication.
Evidence supports using a combination of narrative tasks, picture descriptions, and procedural discourse (Dutta et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Evidence supports using a combination of narrative tasks, picture descriptions, and procedural discourse <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Dutta et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: For direct cross-language comparison, the same discourse tasks should be administered in each language being assessed.
Thus, if two task types are selected, each task should be administered in each language; for a patient assessed in two languages, this would yield four discourse samples.
If the selected tasks do not adequately sample the relevant linguistic structures, discourse genres, or communicative contexts, additional tasks should likewise be administered in each language.

When identical elicitation materials are not culturally or linguistically appropriate across languages, parallel adaptations may be necessary, and those differences should be considered when interpreting performance.
Picture description tasks should also be culturally validated, as the content of the pictures influences narrative production.
What might be culturally familiar or significant to one group may not be to another (Chen et al., 2026).
text.formatted: What might be culturally familiar or significant to one group may not be to another <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Chen et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: For example, widely used narratives such as Cinderella, featured in the AphasiaBank protocol (MacWhinney et al., 2011), may not align with the cultural knowledge or lived experiences of speakers from diverse backgrounds.
text.formatted: For example, widely used narratives such as Cinderella, featured in the AphasiaBank protocol <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">(MacWhinney et al., 2011)</ref>, may not align with the cultural knowledge or lived experiences of speakers from diverse backgrounds.

text.text: When patients are unfamiliar with the content of a task, it may potentially reduce their comfort and/or willingness to produce a detailed discourse sample (Bose et al., 2021).

text.text: Similarly, picture description stimuli can evoke culturally specific interpretations.

Studies have shown that South Asian individuals with Alzheimer's disease, when describing the picnic scene from Western Aphasia Battery-Revised (Kertesz, 2007), interpreted the woman in the image as pouring tea rather than wine, demonstrating how cultural context shapes discourse production (Bose et al., 2021; Dutta, Mello, et al., 2024). Kong (2006) also showed that using the "Cookie Theft" picture description (Goodglass & Kaplan, 1993) for the Chinese population was problematic, as the PWA identified the kitchen scene as a living room and were unable to relate to the theme of stealing cookies from the cookie jar, which led to limited language production and reduced the validity of the task.

text.text: Empirical evidence also demonstrates that culturally relevant stimuli support more complex and productive language output.

For instance, Bengali speakers with and without aphasia produced longer and more complex utterances when describing familiar, realistic color images compared to standard black-and-white line drawings from traditional aphasia batteries (Mazumdar et al., 2020 (Mazumdar et al., , 2023)).

text.text: Because discourse performance may vary across tasks and genres within the same language, no single discourse sample should be assumed to represent an individual's overall discourse abilities.

For bilingual speakers, performance may also differ systematically across languages because of differences in linguistic structure, cultural knowledge, prior experience with the elicitation content, and task demands.

Clinicians should therefore seek converging evidence from multiple discourse tasks in each clinically relevant language and interpret apparent cross-language differences in relation to the cultural and linguistic demands of the tasks.

When normed discourse materials are unavailable, culturally and linguistically adapted tasks may be necessary to obtain representative samples; however, adaptation does not itself establish normative data, psychometric properties, or cross-language equivalence.

Findings from adapted tasks should consequently be interpreted with caution and corroborated with additional discourse samples, language-history information, and other available assessment evidence (Bose et al., 2021 (Bose et al., , 2025;; Dutta et al., 2024 Dutta et al., , 2025)).

text.text: Note.
Listing a language version or adaptation does not indicate that it has equivalent stimuli, normative data, psychometric validation, or cross-language comparability.
Clinicians should verify the status of the specific version and document any modifications used in administration.
Once appropriate discourse tasks have been selected, clinicians must consider linguistically and culturally appropriate administration of the tasks given their contextual constraints.

Clinicians are additionally advised to assess discourse in both monolingual and bilingual modes to determine which context elicits more robust language production and further use this information to develop intervention strategies to facilitate communication in bPWA.
When feasible, language-specific discourse samples should be collected in separate sessions and under conditions that support a relatively monolingual language mode.
For example, the clinician or interpreter can interact exclusively in the target language without signaling use or knowledge of the patient's other language(s).
Collecting samples from different languages in separate sessions may further reduce activation associated with immediately preceding use of another language.

Cross-language responses that nevertheless occur should be documented rather than automatically treated as errors, because difficulty maintaining the target language may itself provide information about lexical retrieval or language control (Grosjean, 2001).
text.formatted: Cross-language responses that nevertheless occur should be documented rather than automatically treated as errors, because difficulty maintaining the target language may itself provide information about lexical retrieval or language control <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Grosjean, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Bilingual-mode samples provide complementary information.

Importantly, clinicians should allow bPWA to use their full linguistic repertoire during assessment, including translanguaging across languages, rather than automatically restricting responses to a single language.

When the patient interacts with someone who shares their languages and is free to use their full linguistic repertoire, this approach more closely reflects how individuals communicate in real-world contexts (Bortz & Goral, 2025).
text.formatted: When the patient interacts with someone who shares their languages and is free to use their full linguistic repertoire, this approach more closely reflects how individuals communicate in real-world contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Bortz & Goral, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This approach also allows clinicians to recognize accurate responses regardless of the language in which they are produced, which can reveal substantially different ability levels compared to single-language assessment scoring (Goral et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This approach also allows clinicians to recognize accurate responses regardless of the language in which they are produced, which can reveal substantially different ability levels compared to single-language assessment scoring <ref type="bibr">(Goral et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, when clinically feasible and time permits, clinicians should consider collecting relatively monolingual-mode and bilingual-mode discourse samples.

Clinicians should document the conditions under which each sample was elicited, including the language(s) used by the clinician, interpreter, or communication partner; the intended language mode; whether unrestricted translanguaging was permitted; and other administration differences that could affect comparisons across samples.
Any translation, adaptation, or modification of instructions, stimuli, prompts, or responses should also be documented, including who performed the translation or adaptation and what was changed.

When the clinician does not speak a language used by the patient, a trained professional interpreter is preferable when available (American Speech-Language-Hearing Association [ASHA], n.d.; Langdon & Saenz, 2016).
text.formatted: When the clinician does not speak a language used by the patient, a trained professional interpreter is preferable when available (American Speech-Language-Hearing Association [ASHA], n.d.; <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">Langdon & Saenz, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Professional interpreters provide language-access expertise and greater independence from the patient than family members or friends; however, clinicians should not assume that interpreters are trained in aphasia, discourse analysis, linguistics, or the administration of speech-language assessments.

The speech-language pathologist (SLP) should therefore brief the interpreter before the session on the purpose and procedures of the assessment, allowable prompting, and the importance of documenting any modifications made during administration, and debrief with the interpreter after the session (Alani et al., 2024; ASHA, n.d.).
text.formatted: The speech-language pathologist (SLP) should therefore brief the interpreter before the session on the purpose and procedures of the assessment, allowable prompting, and the importance of documenting any modifications made during administration, and debrief with the interpreter after the session <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Alani et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">ASHA, n.d.)</ref>.

text.text: When an appropriate professional cannot participate during administration, recorded discourse samples may permit subsequent consultation with another qualified language professional.

Depending on the clinical question, a linguist or other professional with expertise in the relevant language may assist with transcription, segmentation, identification of grammatical and lexical structures, and language-specific interpretation; a professional translator may assist with written transcripts or translations.
These professionals provide linguistic information rather than clinical interpretation, which remains the responsibility of the SLP.

When professional language support cannot be obtained, family members or other communication partners may provide necessary language assistance in addition to their important role in supplying information about premorbid and functional language use.
Because they may lack relevant training and cannot be assumed to be objective, their role and any resulting limitations should be documented and considered in interpretation (ASHA, n.d.).

Potential resources for locating multilingual professionals include https://find.asha.org/pro/  https://www.atanet.org/directory/  https://www.ciol.org.uk/find-a-linguist  https://linguistlist.org/ and university linguistics departments worldwide for language-specific linguistic consultants.

text.text: Discourse samples should be evaluated across languages rather than in isolation (Chen et al., 2026), and multiple levels of language structures such as macrostructure (organization, coherence, and informativeness) and microstructure analyses (morphosyntactic, lexical semantic, and phonological properties) should be assessed within the discourse sample (Sung et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Discourse samples should be evaluated across languages rather than in isolation <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Chen et al., 2026)</ref>, and multiple levels of language structures such as macrostructure (organization, coherence, and informativeness) and microstructure analyses (morphosyntactic, lexical semantic, and phonological properties) should be assessed within the discourse sample <ref type="bibr" target="#b147">(Sung et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Macrostructural analysis examines how effectively an individual conveys and organizes information across utterances and the discourse as a whole (Altman & Goral, 2026).
text.formatted: Macrostructural analysis examines how effectively an individual conveys and organizes information across utterances and the discourse as a whole <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Altman & Goral, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Depending on the discourse task and genre, clinicians may examine informativeness or main concepts (whether essential information is conveyed; Kong, 2011; Ross & Wertz, 1999), local coherence (relations between adjacent utterances), global or topic coherence (maintenance of the overall topic), cohesion (linguistic devices that connect information across utterances), and narrative organization when applicable (Pritchard et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Depending on the discourse task and genre, clinicians may examine informativeness or main concepts (whether essential information is conveyed; <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">Kong, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b137">Ross & Wertz, 1999)</ref>, local coherence (relations between adjacent utterances), global or topic coherence (maintenance of the overall topic), cohesion (linguistic devices that connect information across utterances), and narrative organization when applicable <ref type="bibr" target="#b132">(Pritchard et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: These measures help characterize whether the individual successfully communicates the intended message and organizes it in a way that is interpretable to the listener.

Across a bilingual patient's languages, apparent macrostructural differences should be interpreted in relation to the task, genre, linguistic structure, culturally shaped discourse conventions, and, for conversational samples, culturally and linguistically shaped interactional norms such as turn-taking, topic management, and repair rather than automatically attributed to aphasia (Dutta et al., 2025; Pritchard et al., 2018; Stivers et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Across a bilingual patient's languages, apparent macrostructural differences should be interpreted in relation to the task, genre, linguistic structure, culturally shaped discourse conventions, and, for conversational samples, culturally and linguistically shaped interactional norms such as turn-taking, topic management, and repair rather than automatically attributed to aphasia <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Dutta et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b132">Pritchard et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b146">Stivers et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: For conversational samples, clinicians can additionally examine topic initiation, responsiveness, communicative success, and the distribution of communicative responsibility across speakers (Leaman & Edmonds, 2019 , 2021; Stivers et al., 2009).
text.formatted: For conversational samples, clinicians can additionally examine topic initiation, responsiveness, communicative success, and the distribution of communicative responsibility across speakers <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">(Leaman & Edmonds, 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b146">Stivers et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Microstructural analysis examines linguistic production at the word and utterance/sentence levels, including phonological and lexical properties, morphological marking, and phrase/clause structure (Sung et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Microstructural analysis examines linguistic production at the word and utterance/sentence levels, including phonological and lexical properties, morphological marking, and phrase/clause structure <ref type="bibr" target="#b147">(Sung et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Clinicians can examine phonological errors; lexical retrieval, frequency, and diversity; morphological errors such as incorrect or omitted inflections; phrase/clause structure and grammatical complexity; and utterance/sentence-level measures such as mean length of utterance.
Different patterns of grammatical errors may reflect distinct stages of grammatical encoding (Fahey et al., 2025; Yeaton et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Different patterns of grammatical errors may reflect distinct stages of grammatical encoding <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Fahey et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b156">Yeaton et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: For bilingual discourse assessment, analyzing both macro-and microstructure levels across languages is important because it reveals whether language breakdown patterns are parallel or language-specific.

Where appropriate, coding should include both absolute counts (e.g., total tokens) and proportional measures (e.g., proportion of verbs), because raw output measures may not be directly comparable across languages with different linguistic structures.
For example, a polysynthetic language may encode information that is expressed by multiple words in a more analytic language within a single word (Dryer et al., 2013).
text.formatted: For example, a polysynthetic language may encode information that is expressed by multiple words in a more analytic language within a single word <ref type="bibr">(Dryer et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Clinicians should therefore interpret language-specific features according to the structure of each language while using overlapping structures to support more direct cross-language comparisons.
Parallel impaired performance on comparable structures across languages provides stronger evidence that the underlying linguistic structure is impaired and may identify appropriate treatment targets.

In contrast, differential performance across languages should prompt consideration of premorbid proficiency and use, task and cultural effects, language-specific grammatical properties, and possible impairment of language control before it is interpreted as differential aphasia severity (Chen et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In contrast, differential performance across languages should prompt consideration of premorbid proficiency and use, task and cultural effects, language-specific grammatical properties, and possible impairment of language control before it is interpreted as differential aphasia severity <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Chen et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The proportion of cognates (words that share form and meaning across languages) will be of particular interest, since they are easier for bilinguals to access and their relative frequency is reinforced in each language when used in either language.
When selecting discourse measures for assessment, clinicians should prioritize the measures with documented construct validity and interrater reliability.
Auditory-Perceptual Rating of Connected Speech in Aphasia (APROCSA) provides a transcription-less system for rating multiple speech and language impairment features (Casilio et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Auditory-Perceptual Rating of Connected Speech in Aphasia (APROCSA) provides a transcription-less system for rating multiple speech and language impairment features <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Casilio et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The psychometric properties most relevant to measure selection depend on its intended clinical use: measures used to characterize discourse performance should demonstrate appropriate validity and reliability, whereas measures used to evaluate treatment outcomes should additionally demonstrate adequate test-retest reliability and sensitivity to change.
Literature demonstrates that not all discourse measures are equally robust; some measures are vulnerable to variations in stimulus picture or differences in language groups (Alyahya, 2024).
text.formatted: Literature demonstrates that not all discourse measures are equally robust; some measures are vulnerable to variations in stimulus picture or differences in language groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Alyahya, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, the Arabic Discourse Assessment Tool (ADAT) includes eight discourse measures with strong psychometric properties across both neurotypical and aphasia populations.

These measures include lexical information units, content information units, words per minute, discourse duration, number of different words, number of complete sentences, and proportion of open and closed class words (Alyahya, 2024).
text.formatted: These measures include lexical information units, content information units, words per minute, discourse duration, number of different words, number of complete sentences, and proportion of open and closed class words <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Alyahya, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Another analysis, the main concept analyses (MCA) have the potential to measure skills that have ecological validity of communication abilities (Ross & Wertz, 1999); are sensitive to measuring change in aphasia treatment studies; and have shown good test-retest reliability (i.e., MCA is consistent across multiple administrations) (Kong, 2011).

Selecting measures with documented psychometric properties across the client's languages helps with culturally and linguistically relevant interpretation.

text.text: Because codeswitching may occur at either microstructural or macrostructural levels, its interpretation should be grounded in the cross-language patterns described above as well as the individual's linguistic, cultural, and interactional context.
The location and linguistic unit of each switch, its grammatical integration, its discourse-pragmatic function, and its fit with the interactional context should be considered.

A switch should not be treated as pathological solely because it occurs; language alternation may reflect typical bilingual practice or compensation for lexical retrieval difficulty rather than impaired language control (Mooijman et al., 2025; Neumann et al., 2017).
text.formatted: A switch should not be treated as pathological solely because it occurs; language alternation may reflect typical bilingual practice or compensation for lexical retrieval difficulty rather than impaired language control <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">(Mooijman et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b119">Neumann et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence of impaired control should instead be based on converging observations, such as lack of awareness of switching, switches that conflict with the pragmatic context, or a credible change from premorbid behavior (Gray & Kiran, 2016; Green & Abutalebi, 2008; Mooijman et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Evidence of impaired control should instead be based on converging observations, such as lack of awareness of switching, switches that conflict with the pragmatic context, or a credible change from premorbid behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Gray & Kiran, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Green & Abutalebi, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">Mooijman et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Premorbid switching is difficult to establish because patterns are highly individual and may vary with interlocutor and setting; reports from family members or partners may provide useful context but should not be treated as definitive evidence of the individual's premorbid pattern (Ansaldo & Marcotte, 2007; Myers-Scotton, 2020).
text.formatted: Premorbid switching is difficult to establish because patterns are highly individual and may vary with interlocutor and setting; reports from family members or partners may provide useful context but should not be treated as definitive evidence of the individual's premorbid pattern <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Ansaldo & Marcotte, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b118">Myers-Scotton, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: A credible increase in unintended or context-inappropriate switching, difficulty maintaining a language when the interaction supports a relatively monolingual mode, or reduced ability to modify language choice when cued may contribute evidence of impaired language control.

When such evidence converges across samples and with patient or family/care-partner report, language control may itself warrant consideration as a treatment target (Gray & Kiran, 2016; Green & Abutalebi, 2008; Mooijman et al., 2025).

text.text: Discourse-level analysis of switching can also reveal language-specific lexical or grammatical difficulties that are not apparent on single-word or sentence-level tasks.
Because transcription and discourse coding can be time-and resource-intensive, clinicians may use technology-supported tools to facilitate these processes.
Transcription software and tools can reduce the time required to transcribe discourse samples and aid clinicians' analyses.
Most software is designed for English transcriptions, but certain software, such as VEED.IO, is also freely available for transcription in other languages.

Automated transcription, translation, and analysis are not available or sufficiently accurate for many languages; caution should therefore be used with any automated tool, and automated output should be checked by a proficient human speaker whenever possible (Dutta et al., 2025; Stark & Dalton, 2024).
text.formatted: Automated transcription, translation, and analysis are not available or sufficiently accurate for many languages; caution should therefore be used with any automated tool, and automated output should be checked by a proficient human speaker whenever possible <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Dutta et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b144">Stark & Dalton, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Clinicians can use the aforementioned automated tools for transcribing language samples and thus reducing transcription time; however, these tools do not eliminate the need for appropriate clinical training or language-specific verification.
Automated methods are also available for analyzing the discourse samples.

For example, Computerized Language Analysis (CLAN) software (detailed manuals for coding and analysis freely available at https://aphasia.talkbank.org/) can be used by clinicians for analyzing macrolinguistic variables (e.g., main concepts), and microlinguistic variables (e.g., mean length of utterance, nouns and verbs per utterance, core lexicon) across languages when used in combination with CHAT (Codes for the Human Analysis of Transcripts).

text.text: In summary, best practices for bilingual discourse assessment require clinicians to (a) establish comprehensive language background information; (b) select the same culturally and linguistically appropriate discourse tasks across the languages being assessed, adding multiple task types when needed; (c) collect samples in language modes appropriate to the clinical question and document administration conditions, translations or adaptations, language support, and other modifications; (d) code macrostructural, microstructural, and multilingual discourse features using measures with psychometric properties appropriate to their intended clinical use; (e) interpret cross-language patterns in relation to linguistic structure, premorbid language experience, task and cultural factors, and language control; and (f) integrate converging evidence across available assessment measures, discourse samples, patient and care-partner report, and functional communication; no single source of evidence should determine the clinical interpretation in isolation.

By adopting these evidence-based practices, clinicians can conduct accurate, culturally responsive discourse assessments that reveal the true communicative abilities of bPWA and better inform individualized intervention planning.
>Recommendations for discourse intervention for bilingual aphasia
text.formatted: <head n="4." >Recommendations for discourse intervention for bilingual aphasia</head>

text.text: We believe that the inclusion of discourse treatment offers important benefits over other treatment paradigms.
Discourse-based intervention can directly target functional communication while integrating lexical, morphological, grammatical, and discourse-pragmatic processes within the same activity.

For bPWA, a particular advantage is that more than one language can be incorporated within the same communicative activity, allowing treatment to reflect natural codeswitching, translanguaging, and the language practices of the patient and communication partners.

Discourse activities can also be adapted around culturally relevant topics, routines, interlocutors, and communicative goals rather than relying solely on treatment materials developed for a single language or cultural context.

These features are particularly important given the limited availability of empirically evaluated aphasia treatments across the breadth of languages used by bPWA (Faroqi-Shah et al., 2010; Imaezue et al., 2025).
text.formatted: These features are particularly important given the limited availability of empirically evaluated aphasia treatments across the breadth of languages used by bPWA <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Faroqi-Shah et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Imaezue et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, discourse-focused intervention should be considered a high-priority component of treatment for bPWA, although it can be combined with impairment-based treatment when lexical, morphological, or grammatical impairments also warrant direct treatment.
Providing discourse-level intervention to bPWA presents unique clinical and theoretical challenges.

In addition to typical considerations in discourse treatment, clinicians working with bilingual patients must identify the most appropriate language(s) for treatment, account for variation in premorbid and postmorbid proficiency across languages, and work within the availability of linguistically appropriate therapy materials and language-matched clinicians (Faroqi-Shah et al., 2010).

text.text: Selection of the language(s) targeted in treatment should therefore consider the patient's preferences and everyday communication needs, the availability of language-matched clinical resources, and cross-language generalization.
The patient's language preference should be an important consideration when selecting the language(s) of treatment (Edmonds & Kiran, 2006; Imaezue et al., 2025).

text.text: Cross-language generalization should always be considered in treatment planning, whether treatment is provided in one language or across multiple languages (Ansaldo & Saidi, 2014), because its magnitude and direction vary across individuals, languages, and treatment targets and should not be assumed (Conner et al., 2018; Kuzmina et al., 2019; Lerman et al., 2019).

text.text: When resources permit, directly treating each clinically relevant language reduces reliance on uncertain cross-language transfer; when treatment is limited to fewer languages, clinicians should select targets with the potential for cross-language generalization and measure outcomes in untreated languages.
It is important for clinicians to identify the bPWA's language use across different contexts (e.g., home, work, community) and tailor treatment goals to context-specific functional needs.

The discourse assessment should guide target selection: parallel impairment of comparable structures across languages may support targeting shared linguistic or discourselevel processes, whereas differential impairment may warrant language-specific targets or further consideration of premorbid proficiency, language use, task effects, and language control.
Words and structures with cross-linguistic overlap may be especially useful treatment targets because they may support cross-language generalization.

The factors that predict crosslanguage treatment generalization are not yet well understood (Kuzmina et al., 2019; Lai et al., 2022), but clinicians can consider overlapping structures, including cognates, when clinically appropriate (Falcon & Kurland, 2010; Hameau & Köpke, 2015; Kohnert & Peterson, 2012).

text.text: In such instances, clinicians should consider specific characteristics of each language while translating and adapting a technique developed in one language for use in another.

Adaptation should preserve the therapeutic mechanism while modifying linguistic targets, stimuli, prompts, and expected responses as needed for the lexical, morphological, grammatical, and discourse structures of the language being treated.
Direct translation should not be assumed to produce equivalent treatment targets across languages.
Clinicians should also consider cultural familiarity and communicative relevance when adapting discourse topics or materials.

When comparable or overlapping structures exist across languages, these may be deliberately targeted to support cross-language generalization; when relevant structures are language-specific, treatment should be adapted to those structures rather than forcing equivalence across languages (see Sections 3.1 and 3.3).

Generally, discourse treatments rely on verbal interaction between bPWA and clinicians, which can be compromised when clinicians do not speak the language(s) used by the patient (Larkman et al., 2023).

text.text: Whenever possible, treatment should be delivered by an SLP who is proficient in the target language(s).
When a language-matched SLP is unavailable, multilingual service delivery can be supported through collaboration with a trained professional interpreter or a bilingual co-clinician.
However, ongoing interpreter involvement across a full course of treatment may be constrained by service availability, funding, or cost.

If treatment is available only in a language shared by the patient and SLP, treatment should still be provided rather than withheld; the clinician should select targets with cross-language generalization in mind and assess whether gains extend to the patient's other language(s) (Larkman et al., 2023; Miller Amberber, 2012).

Family members and other regular communication partners can be trained to identify barriers and facilitators, use supportive conversation strategies, and practice those strategies in the language(s) they ordinarily use with the patient.

This role supplements rather than replaces professional treatment or language access and may be particularly valuable when formal treatment is available in only one of the patient's languages (Boles, 2000; Lai et al., 2022).

text.text: Treatment effects should therefore be measured in each clinically relevant language and at the discourse level rather than inferred from improvement in the treated language alone.

Taken together, discourse intervention should be a high-priority component of treatment for bPWA because it can directly target functional communication while incorporating multiple linguistic levels, languages, culturally relevant content, and communication partners within meaningful interactions.

Treatment planning should consider the patient's language preferences and everyday communication needs, the availability of language-matched clinical resources, and the potential for cross-language generalization (Ansaldo & Saidi, 2014; Faroqi-Shah et al., 2010).

text.text: Discourse-focused and impairment-based approaches may also be combined when the patient's goals and impairment profile warrant direct treatment of lexical, morphological, or grammatical processes alongside functional communication.

For bilingual patients, assessment should begin with a comprehensive language history that allows clinicians to consider how the structures of the patient's languages, age and context of acquisition, premorbid proficiency, and patterns of language use may affect language processing before and after the neurological event.
These factors are necessary for distinguishing expected bilingual language patterns from aphasic impairment and for interpreting performance across the patient's languages.
Discourse assessment can then provide converging evidence about functional language performance across languages.

Clinicians should select culturally and linguistically appropriate discourse tasks and, for direct cross-language comparison, administer the same tasks in each language being assessed, adding multiple task types when necessary to represent the patient's discourse abilities.

Administration should consider relatively monolingual and bilingual language modes when clinically feasible and should document the language context, language support, translation or adaptation of materials, and other modifications that may affect interpretation.

Discourse should be analyzed at macrostructural and microstructural levels, while multilingual behaviors such as code-switching should be interpreted in relation to the individual's language history, linguistic structures, cultural and interactional context, and evidence of language control.
Raw and proportional measures, language-specific features, and comparable cross-language structures may provide complementary information.

Clinical conclusions should therefore integrate converging evidence across discourse samples, available assessment measures, patient and care-partner report, and functional communication rather than relying on any single source of evidence.

For intervention, discourse should be considered a high-priority treatment component because it can directly target functional communication while integrating multiple linguistic levels, languages, culturally relevant content, and communication partners within meaningful interactions.
Treatment-language decisions should consider patient preference, everyday communication needs, available clinical resources, and cross-language generalization.

When feasible, treatment of each clinically relevant language reduces reliance on uncertain crosslanguage transfer; however, treatment should not be withheld when services are available in only one or some of the patient's languages.
In those circumstances, clinicians should consider crosslanguage generalization when selecting targets and evaluate outcomes across the patient's languages.

Treatment materials and approaches should be adapted to language-specific and cultural characteristics rather than directly translated, and communication-partner training can extend communication support into languages and contexts outside the formal treatment environment (Ansaldo & Saidi, 2014; Bihovsky et al., 2025; Boles, 2000; Faroqi-Shah et al., 2010; Lai et al., 2022; Lerman et al., 2019).

text.text: With standardized assessments and treatments available in only a limited number of languages (Wallace et al., 2022) and targeting a limited number of language structures, incorporating discourse measures may be an especially useful approach to assess and treat bilingual populations.

text.text: Despite limited research on clinical bilingual populations, we have offered practice guidelines for use of discourse in assessment and treatment based on available evidence.

This evidence originates from studies of healthy bilingual processing and bilingual identity, research on bilingual aphasia and cross-language treatment, evidence concerning differences between bilingual language patterns and aphasic deficits, available clinical tools, and the broader evidence base for discourse assessment and intervention.
These recommendations are necessarily constrained by the current evidence base.

Studies of bilingual aphasia frequently include small samples or individual cases, represent a limited range of languages and language combinations, and vary substantially in assessment tasks, treatment approaches, and outcome measures.

Normative and psychometric evidence is also uneven across languages, and some recommendations necessarily draw on converging evidence from healthy bilingual language processing or the broader aphasia literature where direct evidence in bPWA is unavailable.

The recommendations should therefore be applied in relation to the linguistic, cultural, clinical, and resource context of the individual patient rather than interpreted as prescriptive rules applicable uniformly across multilingual populations.

Future research should consider the psychometric qualities of discourse analysis tools and the development of standardized discourse measures relevant to bilingual populations, systematically examine mechanisms of cross-language treatment generalization, and conduct larger, more methodologically rigorous treatment studies across diverse language combinations.

Research should also expand the linguistic and cultural diversity of discourse tasks and treatment studies, evaluate approaches to multilingual service delivery when language-matched clinicians are unavailable, and identify which discourse measures are most sensitive to clinically meaningful within-and cross-language treatment change.

Such studies will be necessary to generate evidence that reflects the linguistic complexity of aphasia in bilinguals and to establish robust guidelines that support equitable and effective discourse rehabilitation for bPWA.
